How easy are the syntheses of allenes?
Shichao Yu a and Shengming Ma* ab
Received 17th December 2010, Accepted 18th February 2011
DOI: 10.1039/c0cc05640e
Allenes have proven themselves to be valuable building blocks toward complex molecular targets,
revealing novel applications in natural product synthesis, pharmaceutical chemistry and materials
science. The ongoing interest in allene chemistry results in a variety of new methodologies and
pathways for the synthesis of allenes. This feature article highlights some of the recent important
developments on the synthesis of allenes and the applications on the synthesis of allenic natural
products and allenic-based optoelectronic materials.
Introduction
In the past few decades, allene chemistry has experienced a
veritable explosion. 1 Their synthetic potential in regio- and
stereoselective C–C and C–X bond-forming transformations,
unique axis-to-center chirality transfer, occurrence of allenic
structures in a variety of natural products and pharmacologically
active compounds, have inspired ample interest of organic and
medicinal chemists. Thus, the synthesis of allenes will surely be
a hot research topic for the next decades.
2 All the classical
reaction types (addition, elimination, substitution, rearrangement)
have been applied to the synthesis of allenes and transition-
metal catalyzed allene synthesis have also been developed.
However, catalytic stereoselective variations are still challenging
and an under-represented area of synthetic organic chemistry.
3
This feature article highlights some of the recent important
developments on the synthesis of allenes with a brief touch on
the history, which have not been included in the recent
reviews1n,2e,4 and is organized according to the starting
materials and categorized further by reaction types.

a common class of reactions used to access allenes

(Scheme 1).5 For example, allenes can be obtained by dehydro-
halogenation of 2-halopropene derivatives using strong bases, 6
syn-selenoxide elimination of vinyl selenides, 7 and metal-
promoted reduction of 2,3-dihalopropene or b-haloallyl alcohol
derivatives.8 Recently, 2,3-dichloro-1-propene eliminating
two molecules of KCl in the presence of K 2Te2 to aﬀord
propadiene has also been reported. 9
This elimination protocol has been recently applied to the
synthesis of 1,1-diﬂuoroallenes (Scheme 2). 10 Upon treatment
with n-butyl lithium, 2-bromo-3,3-diﬂuoroallylic acetates 1
underwent lithium-bromide exchange, followed by 1,2-elimination
of lithium acetate to aﬀord mono- and disubstituted 1,1-
diﬂuoroallenes 2 in high yields. The corresponding starting
material could be prepared conveniently from the reaction of
aldehydes or ketones with 1-bromo-2,2-diﬂuorovinyl lithium.
The use of hexane was essential since it is a nonpolar solvent
resulting in a higher degree of aggregation of lithium reagents.
Its low reactivity helped to suppress undesired side reactions.
Similarly, Yamazaki et al. used zinc-mediated 1,2-elimination
of 2-iodo-3-triﬂuoromethylallylic acetates to prepare the
potentially important CF
3-substituted allenes. 11
Based on Knochel’s Mg–Br exchange protocol, Wu et al.
have reported an enantioselective synthesis of 1,3-disubtituted
allenes 5 from optically active ethyl 6 -acetoxy-5-iodotetradeca-
2,4-dienoate 4 in good yield and a high level of stereoselectivity
(Scheme 3).
12
The oxidative syn-elimination reaction of ( Z)-3-phenyl-
seleno-3-alkenyl methyl ethers 6 with mCPBA furnished
functionalized allene derivatives 7 in good yields
(Scheme 4). 13 The conﬁguration of the C QC bond was
important for the formation of allenes since the corresponding
selenoxide elimination of ( E)-3-phenylselenohomoallylic
ethers exclusively gave alkyne derivatives.
The reaction of 1-chlorovinyl sulfoxides 9 with iPrMgCl
gave a magnesium species 11 via sulfoxide-magnesium
exchange (Scheme 5).
14 Treatment of this magnesium carbenoid
with 2-lithio-5-methoxyfuran resulted in the formation of
functionalized allenes 10 in moderate yields.
Furthermore, when magnesium species 15 were trapped by
lithium enolates of a-chloroalkanoates, fully substituted
2,3-allenonates 14 could be obtained in 17–51% yield
(Scheme 6).
15
Treatment of b-ketoesters 17 with 2 equiv. of LiHMDS and
Tf2O formed vinyl enolate intermediates 19. Subsequent
addition of another equivalent of LiHMDS, 3 equiv. of
HMPA, and ZnCl
2 led to terminal 2,3-allenoates 18 in good
yields (Scheme 7). 16
Surprisingly, Bertrand et al. synthesized the highly strained
cationic 4-membered allenes 21 bearing two piperidino groups
by alkylation of 3-ethoxyspiro[3,5]non-2-en-1-one 20 with
Et3O.BF4, followed by addition of excess piperidine
(Scheme 8). 17 Upon lithiation at /C020 1C, cyclic allenes 22
were cleanly produced. This compound is highly reactive and
stable only for several hours at /C020 1C. This strategy has also
been applied to the synthesis of 5-membered cyclic allenes 24
and 25 (Scheme 9). 18
1.2 By intramolecular eliminative H-migration
Upon treatment of the tosylhydrazone derivatives 28 generated
in situ from the reaction of a,b-unsaturated enones 26 with
tosylhydrazine, allenes 27 were produced with loss of N 2 and
intramolecular H-transfer of the diazene intermediate 29
(Scheme 10). 19
1.3 By Wittig and related reactions
Wittig reaction is an important method for the formation of
CQC bonds. 20 The reaction of phosphonium ylides and
ketenes has been employed to access a variety of functionalized
allenes, including allenyl esters,
21 ketones,22 lactones and
lactams etc.23 To avoid the manipulation of unstable ketenes,
their equivalents, such as acid halides 24 or aryl esters, 25 are
commonly used.
Palladium-catalyzed allylic alkylation of phosphorus ylides
30 in the presence of a Pd/Trost ligand system aﬀorded a new
class of allylic phosphorus ylides 34, which reacted with
various ketenes furnishing tetrasubstituted allenes 32 in
moderate to good overall yields (Scheme 11). 26
Petasis oleﬁnation, involving conversion of carbonyl
compounds to oleﬁns, is an important process for construction
of C–C double bonds in organic synthesis.
27 The use of
alkenylidene titanocene provides a direct and versatile way
to prepare a variety of allenes from aldehydes or ketones.
28
Recently, Zhou et al. reported a tandem reaction starting
from allylgallation of magnesium acetylides, followed by the
reaction with aldehydes to aﬀord allyl allenes 37 in moderate
yields (Scheme 12).
29
When a-silyl a-diazo ketones 39 and silyl ketenes 40 were
combined at 0–20 1C for 3–12 h, 1,3-diaryl-3-silyl-1-silyloxy-
allenes 41 were formed in fairly good yields (Scheme 13). 30 The
reaction might proceed via cyclopropanonation of silyl
ketenes 40 with 1-diazo-2-silyloxyethenes 42, followed by
decarbonylation to yield 1,3-diaryl-1-silyloxy-3-silylallenes 41.
1.4 By C–C bond cleavage
C–C fragmentation has been less explored in the preparation
of allenes. In 2005, Nagao et al. developed a strategy for the
synthesis of chained keto allenoates by retro-Dieckmann-
type
31 or retro-aldol-type 32 reactions of a-alkynyl-a-ethoxy-
carbonyl cyclopentanone and cyclohexanone derivatives
under basic conditions. Recently, Williams and co-workers have
shown that b-siloxy substituted vinyl triﬂates 44 smoothly
underwent C–C fragmentation to aﬀord trisubstituted allenes
45 stereoselectively in the presence of TBAF (Scheme 14).
33
Nucleophile-induced Grob-type fragmentation 34 reactions
of vinylogous acyl triﬂates 47 leading to b-functionalized
allenes 48 were developed by Cramer et al. 35 The reaction
led to trisubstituted allenes with carbonyl functionality at the
oxidation level of a carboxylic acid (Scheme 15).

1.5 By allylic substitution of 2-halo-1,3-butadienes
The transition metal-catalyzed reactions of 2-halo-1,3-dienes
with various nucleophiles, such as sodium malonates, sodium
phenoxides, or potassium amides, provide a highly selective
and practical tool for the synthesis of a-functionalized allenes
(Scheme 16). 3b,36 The most commonly used transition metals
are organocopper and palladium(0) complexes. For the former,
organocuprates usually act as nucleophiles to react with
2-halo-1,3-butadienes1-III via S
N20 or SN2 processes furnishing
allenes 1-VI or 1,3-butadiene derivatives 1-V, respectively.
As for the latter, (alkylidene- p-allyl)palladium is the key
intermediate. Attacking the 1- or 3-position of this intermediate
aﬀords the corresponding allenes 1-VI or 1,3-dienes 1-V.
Many factors such as solvents, temperature aﬀect the regio-
selectivities. Highly enantioselective preparation of axial chiral
allenic compounds could also be achieved by the use of chiral
phosphines.
37

2. From alkynes
Alkynes, isomers of allenes, are probably the most widely used
starting materials for the synthesis of allenes.
39
2.1 By isomerization of alkynes
Isomerization of the FG–CH 2–CRC moiety in the presence
of a base is one of the earliest methods for access to allenes
(Scheme 18).
40 Simple alkynes are usually treated with
strong bases such as alkali metal amide (NaNH 2) at a high
temperature.41 For alkynes with activated a-hydrogen or
coordination to a transition metal, weaker bases such as
NaOH, KO tBu and TBAF are enough to facilitate the
isomerization.
42 The activation groups include alkene, 43
arene,44 alkyne,45 or carbonyl group, 46 or groups containing
oxygen,47 nitrogen,48 sulfur,49 or phosphorus atom. 50
Polychloro bridged bicyclic propargyl alcohols 54
isomerized to the corresponding allenols 55 in the presence
of powdered KOH in benzene at 80 1C with 80–85% yields
(Scheme 19). 51

Propargylic tosylates 56 with the CF 3 group at the terminal
sp carbon atom isomerized to allenyl tosylates 57 smoothly at
room temperature in the presence of sodium hydroxides in a
water–organic biphasic solvent system (Scheme 20).
52
Quite excitingly, an enantioselective isomerization of
3-alkynonates 58 to optically active 2,3-dienonates 60 with
chiral bicyclic guanidine 59 as base was also developed
(Scheme 21). 53
Oxidation/isomerization of homopropargyl alcohols is a
convenient way for synthesis of a-allenyl ketones. 54 Recently,
Fan et al. reported a green catalytic system using RuCl 3 in
ionic liquid with tert-butyl hydroperoxide (TBHP) as the
oxidant (Scheme 22). 55
The coupling reaction of a-methyl benzylbromide 63 with
the trialkynylindium derivative of ethyl propiolate 64 in the
presence of chiral nickel complex aﬀorded axially chiral allene
65 in 30% yield with good enantioselectivity (77% ee)
(Scheme 23).
56 Other alkynylindium derivatives with aryl,
vinyl and TMS substituents gave benzyl-substituted alkynes.
2.2 By S N20-substitution
Substitution reaction of propargylic compounds with a leaving
group is the most commonly employed and convenient
method for the synthesis of allenes (Scheme 24).
57 In many
cases, non-racemic propargylic substrates proceed in a stereo-
selective manner. A variety of labile groups, including
propargylic acetates, mesylates, carbonates, and halides, etc.
have been used as leaving groups.
58
2.2.1 Substitution by nucleophile reagents. Haloallenes are
useful substrates for substitution reactions 59 and transition
metal-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions. 60 They have also
been found in many natural products. 61 A variety of reaction
conditions for the preparation of haloallenes from propargyl
alcohols have been developed.
62
Treatment of aryl-substituted propargyl alcohols 66 with
N-halosuccinimide and triphenylphosphine aﬀorded chloro- or
bromoallenes 68 in moderate to good yields and high regio-
selectivities (Scheme 25). 63
Appel-type reaction conditions containing Ph 3P, CBr 4,
(n-Bu)3P, and i-Pr2NEt were also applied to the bromination
of 1-arylpropargylic alcohol 69 aﬀording allenyl bromides
70.64 Bromination of CF 3-substituted propargylic alcohols
71 by the combined reagents CBr 4–Ph3P gave bromoallenes
72 (Scheme 26). 65
Haloallenes can also be prepared from propargyl boronates
(Scheme 27). 66 Treatment of propargyl diethanolamine
boronates73 with N-halosuccinimides74 gave the corresponding
allenyl bromides 75 in high yields.
The reaction of secondary or tertiary propargylic alcohols
76 with NbBr 5 aﬀorded allenylic bromides 78 in moderate to
good yields (Scheme 28). 67 The halides were readily isolated in
pure form through simple extraction and could be used
directly in subsequent transformation.
Synthesis of optically active bromoallene 80 by treatment of
enantioenriched propargyl tosylate or mesylate 79 with LiBr
and CuBr in THF was developed by Montury and Gore ´ in
1980.
68 During Wu’s recent investigations, 69 they noticed that
the enantiopurity of the bromoallenes could change dramatically
from run to run (Scheme 29). After systematic screening on the
reaction conditions, they found that Cu( II) species played an
unexpected role in improving the enantioselectivity in this
particular transformation. Commercially available ‘anhydrous’
diethyl ether (with H
2O content o0.3%) was a much better
solvent than THF, which was the only solvent that has been
used for this reaction up to now. The newly established
conditions (addition of 0.1 equiv. of Cu(OTf)
2 with Et 2Ot o
replace THF) increased the regioselectivity from 1.5 : 1
[S
N20/SN2] to 3.8 : 1 and the er from 13 : 1 (85% ee) to 46 : 1
(96% ee).
DBU reacts with CO 2 to form DBU–CO 2 zwitterionic
carbamic complex 83, which has been observed for various
carbon dioxide ﬁxation reactions. 70 Yoshida and Ihara et al.
applied this species to the synthesis of oxazolidinones starting
from 4-(benzylamino)-2-butynyl carbonates and benzoates 82
(Scheme 30).
71 5-Vinylideneoxazolidin-2-ones 85 were
obtained in good yields under palladium-free conditions.
The reaction of 2-aryindoles 86 with tertiary propargylic
alcohols 87 in the presence of Brønsted acid gave 3-allenylindole
derivatives 88 in moderate to good yields (Scheme 31). 72 The
competitive isomerization of the resulted allenes to dienes
process could be slowed down when the substituents at the
propargylic position is secondary alkyl groups. 1,3-Dicarbonyl
derivatives reacted with tertiary propargylic alcohols also
giving similar results.
73
Syntheses of allenes from propargylic alcohols can also be
realized by using appropriate activating reagents. For example,
phosphane-like PPh
3 was employed as a nucleophile and
deoxygenation reagent eﬃciently to promote the transformation
of 2,4-alkadiynols 89 into allenynes 90 (Scheme 32).
74 The
hydrogen was proposed to transfer intramolecularly from the
hydroxyl group. The presence of a conjugated alkynyl group is
necessary for the conversion of a propargyl alcohol into an
allene, as propargyl alcohols with only one alkynyl group
resulted in no reaction with the recovering of the starting
materials.
One eﬃcient access to allenes is base-mediated desilylation
of propargyl silanes.
75 With 1.5 equiv of TBAF in THF at
room temperature, the TMS-substituted propargyl alcohols 91
were transformed into the 2,3-allenols 92 in good to excellent
yields (Scheme 33). 76

2.2.2 Substitution with organometallic reagents. Organo-
copper-mediated S N20 substitution reactions are one of the
most versatile and popular synthetic routes to allenes. 58a,b,77
The easily available diorganocuprates (Gilman’s cuprates) are
commonly used reactive copper reagents. Catalytic variants
involving the use of Grignard reagents with a small amount of
copper(
I) salt have also been developed, which avoids the
usually observed formation of acetylenic derivatives resulting
from direct S
N2 nucleophilic substitution. 78
2.2.2.1 Stoichiometric or ganocopper reagents as nucleophiles.
Triﬂuorovinyl, perﬂuorophenyl or ( Z)-pentaﬂuoropropenyl
copper reagents 93 readily reacted with tertiary propargylic
chlorides 94 to give perﬂuoro-substituted allenes 95 stereoselec-
tively in good yields (Scheme 34).79

Enantiomerically enriched allenyl silanes 97 have been
produced stereoselectively by treatment of enantiopure
oxazolidine propargyl acetate 96 with (trimethylsilyl)cyano-
cuprate 98 via an anti-S
N20 substitution process (Scheme 35). 80
Treatment of propargyl bromides or mesylates 100 with a
chiral sulfoxide 99 containing benzylic copper complexes
aﬀorded the chiral allenes 101 by an anti S N20 process
(Scheme 36). 81 The sulﬁnyl group eﬃciently transferred its
chiral information to the products. When optically active
propargyl mesylates were subjected to the reaction, up to
95/5 diastereoselectivity was observed.
2.2.2.2 Copper( I)-catalyzed nucleophilic substitution.
Cu-catalyzed nucleophilic substitution reactions exhibited
higher yields and selectivities than analogous stoichiometric
amounts of Cu(
I) salt-mediated reactions. Commonly used
organometallic reagents included organolithium, 82 Grignard
reagents,83 organozinc84 and organozirconium, 85 etc.
Groth et al. developed an approach towards enantio-
merically enriched a-allenylglycines 105 utilizing homocuprate
of the bislactim ether of cyclo-(–L-Val–Gly–) 102 and primary
propargyl halides 103 (Scheme 37). 86 This copper-catalyzed
SN20 substitution produces the allenyl-substituted bislactim
ethers 104 in a highly diastereoselective manner, albeit,
the yields are not high due to the formation of the S N2
substitution products. Subsequent hydrolysis of the allenyl-
substituted dihydropyrazines 104 aﬀords the a-allenylglycines
105.
Copper(
I)-catalyzed anti-SN20-type reduction of propargylic
carbonates with hydrosilanes to various di- and trisubstituted
allenes have been reported.
87,88 NHC ligands (Scheme 38) 87b
or phosphine ligands (Scheme 39) 88 were used to stabilize the
corresponding CuH complexes. These reactions have a good
tolerance to various functional groups and work eﬃciently for
the synthesis of optically active allenes.
When the hydride source was replaced by bis-pinacolato
diboron 113, various allenylboronates 114 could be aﬀorded
eﬃciently. The Cu(
I)/Xantphos system also worked well for
the preparation of axially chiral allenylboronate 116 from an
optically active propargylic carbonate 115 (Scheme 40). 89
Propargylic derivatives bearing an alkoxy leaving group
have been used for access to polyalkylpropa-1,2-dienes, 78a
1,2,4,6-tetraenes90 and a-allenylamines.91 For synthesis of
chiral 2,3-allenols, optically active 4-hydroxy-4-aryl-2-butynyl
methyl ethers 117 were subjected to primary alkyl Grignard
reagents under the catalysis of CuBr (Scheme 41).
92
Enantioenriched 2-substituted secondary 2,3-allenols 118 were
obtained with up to >99% ee. However, the yields were
somewhat low and the 4-substituent groups were limited to
aryl groups.
Then, the related propargyl chlorides 119 were employed to
overcome those shortcomings for the above mentioned
copper(
I)-catalyzed nucleophilic substitution (Scheme 42). 93
2.2.2.3 Organocopper-mediated ring-opening reactions. The
organocopper-mediated ring-opening reaction of alkynylic
epoxides,82,94 lactones95 or cyclic carbonate 96 aﬀords the
corresponding allenols in high regio- and anti-diastereo-
selectivity. Recently, this strategy was applied to the synthesis
of bisallenols 122 (Scheme 43).
97 Addition of Grignard
reagents with a catalytic amount of CuBr to bis(acetylenic
epoxides) 121 led to conjugated bisallenols 122. The reaction
proceeded in two steps and monosubstitution products could
be isolated at very low temperatures.
Treatment of acetylenic dioxolanones with organo-
magnesium cuprate reagents aﬀorded a-allenols in good to
excellent yields (Scheme 44).
98
2.2.3 Substitution by other organometallic reagents .99 Allyl
indium reagents, generated in situ from indium and allyl
bromides 127, reacted with tertiary propargyl alcohols 126
aﬀording tri- and tetra-substituted allenes 128 in good yields
(Scheme 45). 100
When propargyl bromide 129 and chlorosilane were
treated with 1 equiv. of indium powder in DMF at room
temperature, allenylsilane 130 were produced highly selectively
(Scheme 46).

Allenes can be synthesized via the direct S N20 addition of
hydride to propargylic alcohols. Especially, aluminum hydride
reagents, such as lithium aluminum hydride (LiAlH
4), and
diisobutylaluminum hydride (DIBAL-H), have been widely
used to prepare allenes from propargyl moieties such as ethers,
halides, alcohols and epoxides.
102 Recently, Cp 2Zr(H)Cl has
been applied to the anti-S N20-type reductive substitution of the
in situ generated zinc or magnesium alkoxides of propargylic
alcohols 131 furnishing allenes 132 in good yields and in high
optical purities (Scheme 47). 103 This approach provides direct
and stereospeciﬁc access to allenes directly from propargylic
alcohols and therefore greatly improved the eﬃciency.
The rhodium-catalyzed related reactions have also been
reported.
104 With the success on the synthesis of allenyl-
boronates, Sawamura et al. developed a Rh-catalyzed coupling
reaction between propargylic carbonates 133 and silyl-
boronates 134 aﬀording allenylsilanes 135 with high yields
(Scheme 48).105 The reaction of an optically active propargylic
carbonate 136 took place in the presence of [Rh(cod) 2][BF4]
(10 mol%) giving allenylsilanes 137 in 77% yield. From the
result of TiCl 4-mediated addition of this allenylsilane to
isobutyraldehyde, it was concluded that the center-to-axial
chirality transfer in the Rh-catalyzed coupling proceeded with
an anti stereochemistry.
Other organometallic reagents, such as organozinc, also
reacted with propargylic compounds to form allenes
(Scheme 49). It was found that DMSO solvent could
dramatically improve the regioselectivity of the S
N20 reactions
of propargyl mesylates 139 with organozinc reagents. By using
LiCl-free diorganozinc, stereoselective conversion of chiral
substrates 141 was also achieved.
106
Nickel(II)-catalyzed substitution of propargylic compounds
143 with intramolecular carbon nucleophiles aﬀorded indene
derivatives 144 with an allene moiety in moderate to
excellent yields (Scheme 50). 107 The reaction was initiated by
nucleometallation of CRC triple bond, followed by elimination
of Ni–OR 3 bond.
Direct substitution of the hydroxy group in propargylic
alcohols with nucleophiles provides an atom eﬃcient and
environmentally sound way for the introduction of alkyne or
allene group into a molecule.
108 Zhou et al. developed a
FeCl3/C16H2O catalyzed intramolecular substitution reaction

Conclusions
With these recent highlighted examples we hope to raise the
reader’s attention to this exciting chemistry and convinced
him/her that allenes are no longer chemist curiosities. The
applications of allenes in the total synthesis, medicinal
chemistry and advanced materials will spur much interest into
both the synthesis of allenes as well as their further applications.
Great advances have been achieved with the development of
new catalytic systems and more ligands available now. A
variety of new methods for complex, multi-functionalized,
especially chiral allenes have been developed. Revitalizing
‘‘the old’’ reactions leads to wider substrate scope, milder
reaction conditions, ﬁnely-tuned regio- and stereoselectivities
and even new synthesis for allenes. New sources of starting
material have also been explored; nevertheless alkynes still
dominate this territory. One problem not yet been fully
resolved is the lack of proper and simple methods for supplying
enantiomerically enriched compounds from readily available
starting material. Currently, the synthesis of enantiomerically
enriched allenes has relied on the transfer of chirality from
a stereogenic center to the allene axis, optical resolution
of racemic allenes, and recently, catalytic enantioselective
synthesis of chiral allenes.
24,25 New approaches from readily
available chemicals are highly desirable, which should lead to
further applications of allenes in stereoselective syntheses,
especially in those of natural products, pharmaceuticals, and
material science. In the future, this point will probably
constitute the most exciting challenge waiting for chemists to
conquer.
